subject: Medicine
summary: Nutrition is a cornerstone of health, influencing disease risk, recovery and mortality. In low‑resource East African hospitals clinicians must assess, diagnose and manage malnutrition with limited investigations.

sections.p: Nutrition refers to the intake, absorption and utilization of nutrients required for growth, maintenance and repair. Clinical malnutrition is diagnosed when anthropometry or clinical signs indicate inadequate nutrient stores.
b: BMI <18.5 kg/m² in adults
Mid‑upper arm circumference (MUAC) <23 cm (women) or <22 cm (men)
Weight loss >10 % in 3–6 months

sections.p: The WHO/UNICEF Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) classification is used for adults and children.
b: Moderate acute malnutrition: BMI 16–16.9 kg/m² or MUAC 21–22.9 cm
Severe acute malnutrition: BMI <16 kg/m² or MUAC <21 cm
Chronic malnutrition: stunting (height‑for‑age <‑2 SD) in children

sections.p: In East Africa, the most common drivers are socioeconomic, infectious and chronic disease related.
b: Food insecurity and poverty
Chronic infections: HIV, TB, malaria, schistosomiasis
Gastrointestinal losses: chronic diarrhoea, parasitic infections
Malabsorption: celiac disease, pancreatic insufficiency
Increased metabolic demand: severe burns, trauma, surgery
Medication effects: antiretrovirals, anti‑TB drugs causing nausea

sections.p: Patients may appear thin, have loss of subcutaneous fat, muscle wasting, edema, or skin changes.
b: Visible loss of muscle bulk (temples, clavicles)
Dry, thin hair and brittle nails
Koilonychia (spoon nails)
Peripheral edema in severe protein deficiency
Fatigue, poor wound healing, recurrent infections

t.b: Is the patient underweight? – Confirms chronic energy deficiency
Is there acute malnutrition? – Quick bedside screen when scales unavailable
Is there protein‑energy deficiency? – Low <30 g/L suggests severe malnutrition but may be affected by inflammation
Is there anemia or infection? – Microcytic anemia points to iron deficiency; leukocytosis may indicate infection
Which vitamins/minerals are deficient? – Low ferritin, vitamin D, B12 guide supplementation
Is there parasitic loss? – Positive result directs anti‑helminth therapy

sections.p: Severe malnutrition can rapidly become life‑threatening.
b: Refeeding syndrome (electrolyte shifts on nutrition re‑initiation)
Severe edema or ascites indicating hypoalbuminemia
Impaired immunity leading to sepsis
Cardiac failure from thiamine deficiency (wet beriberi)
Delayed wound healing and pressure sores

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then provide safe nutritional rehabilitation.
b: Treat infections first (e.g., start anti‑TB therapy, antiretrovirals).
Correct electrolyte abnormalities before feeding (especially potassium, phosphate, magnesium).
Start low‑energy, high‑protein oral therapeutic foods (e.g., Plumpy’Nut, locally prepared millet‑based porridge).
If oral intake impossible, use nasogastric feeding with 10‑15 kcal/kg/day, advancing slowly.
Avoid high‑dose glucose solutions alone to prevent refeeding hypophosphatemia.

sections.p: Nutrition status must be monitored regularly and underlying risk factors addressed.
b: Weekly weight and MUAC checks during refeeding.
Educate caregivers on balanced diets using locally available foods.
Screen for HIV, TB and parasitic infections annually.
Promote food‑security programmes and agricultural support.
Vaccinate against measles, pneumococcus and influenza to reduce infection‑related wasting.
Hyperthyroidism – weight loss with tremor and tachycardia, not loss of fat stores.
Chronic heart failure – cachexia but accompanied by peripheral edema and raised JVP.
Depression – reduced intake but usually without physical signs of muscle wasting.
Serum albumin falls in inflammation; a normal level does not exclude malnutrition.
BMI may be misleading in oedematous patients; use MUAC instead.
Micronutrient assays often unavailable; clinical signs guide empiric supplementation.

whenToSeekHelp: Altered mental status after starting feeds (suspect refeeding syndrome)
Unexplained fever or sepsis in a malnourished patient

faq.q: Can a patient with normal BMI still be malnourished?
faq.a: Yes; edema or high muscle mass can mask low fat stores, so MUAC and clinical signs are essential.
Rapid carbohydrate intake drives insulin, causing phosphate, potassium and magnesium shifts that can precipitate cardiac arrest.

faq.q: What is the first step if a laboratory test is unavailable?
faq.a: Rely on bedside anthropometry (BMI, MUAC) and clinical signs to guide immediate management.

exam: What bedside measurements would you use to screen for acute malnutrition in a 3‑year‑old child when scales are unavailable? — MUAC; <12.5 cm indicates moderate, <11.5 cm severe.

A 45‑year‑old HIV‑positive man presents with BMI 15 kg/m² and peripheral edema. What is your immediate management priority? — Correct electrolytes and start low‑calorie feeding to avoid refeeding syndrome before aggressive caloric increase.
How does chronic malaria contribute to malnutrition, and what investigations would you order? — Repeated haemolysis and appetite loss; order malaria smear, full blood count and stool for parasites.

Explain why serum albumin is not a reliable sole marker of nutritional status in an acutely ill patient. — It falls with inflammation and fluid shifts, giving a false impression of protein deficiency.
When would you choose nasogastric feeding over oral therapeutic foods in a malnourished patient? — When the patient cannot protect the airway, has severe oral lesions, or is unconscious.
Identify two micronutrients most commonly deficient in East African malnutrition and their clinical signs. — Iron (microcytic anemia, fatigue) and vitamin A (night blindness, xerophthalmia).
What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent referral for a malnourished child with suspected refeeding syndrome? — New onset cardiac arrhythmia or severe weakness with hypophosphatemia.
Distinguish between protein‑energy malnutrition and wet beriberi in an alcoholic patient. — Both have edema, but wet beriberi shows high-output cardiac failure and responds to thiamine.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused nutritional history combined with a systematic physical exam reveals the severity and aetiology of malnutrition and distinguishes it from other wasting disorders.
b: Duration of weight loss (weeks vs months) and recent changes in appetite or food intake.
Food security: household income, access to meals, recent famine or displacement.
Recent infections (TB, HIV, malaria, diarrhoea), chronic diseases (cancer, CKD), and surgeries or burns.
Medication history: antiretrovirals, anti‑TB drugs, diuretics, steroids, or traditional remedies.
Pregnancy status, lactation, and infant feeding practices (breast‑feeding, complementary foods).
Alcohol use, tobacco, and substance abuse that may impair absorption.
Social support, caregiver capacity, and cultural beliefs about food.

t.b: Ask: Is there visible loss of subcutaneous fat? Positive: prominent ribs, clavicles, temporal wasting; indicates chronic energy deficit. Cannot quantify severity without measurements.

Ask: What is the arm circumference? Adults: <22 cm (men) or <23 cm (women) = severe; 22‑22.9 cm or 23‑23.9 cm = moderate. Children 6‑59 mo: <11.5 cm severe, 11.5‑12.5 cm moderate. Positive indicates acute malnutrition; does not assess micronutrient status.
Ask: Height and weight? BMI <16 kg/m² = severe acute malnutrition; 16‑16.9 kg/m² = moderate. BMI does not reflect fluid overload; edema can mask low BMI.
Ask: Is there pitting edema? Grade 1+ in both feet suggests protein deficiency; severe (≥2+) may indicate hypoalbuminaemia or cardiac/renal disease. Edema can falsely elevate weight and BMI.
Ask: Are hair dry, brittle, or nails spoon‑shaped? Koilonychia and hair changes support protein‑energy malnutrition; they are not specific for micronutrient deficiency.
Ask: Is there shifting dullness? Positive indicates fluid accumulation, often from hypoalbuminaemia; bedside test cannot differentiate cause without paracentesis.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Laboratory and imaging studies confirm the nutritional deficit, uncover underlying disease, and guide re‑feeding. When a test is unavailable, use clinical surrogates.
b: Serum albumin and pre‑albumin – assess protein status but are negative acute‑phase reactants; low values may reflect infection or inflammation.
Complete blood count – anaemia pattern (microcytic → iron deficiency; macrocytic → folate/B12).
Serum electrolytes, phosphate, magnesium – baseline before re‑feeding; watch for refeeding syndrome.
Serum zinc, selenium, thiamine – targeted micronutrient checks when clinical signs suggest deficiency.
Stool microscopy and ova‑parasite exam – detect helminths or protozoa causing malabsorption.
HIV rapid test, GeneXpert for TB – rule out chronic infections driving wasting.
Chest X‑ray or abdominal ultrasound – identify chronic lung disease, ascites, or organomegaly when physical exam is equivocal.

t.b: Does the patient have hypoalbuminaemia? <30 g/L suggests inflammation or protein loss; not reliable alone for nutritional status. If unavailable, use clinical edema and MUAC.
Is phosphate <0.8 mmol/L after feeding? Low phosphate signals re‑feeding syndrome; treat with supplementation. If lab not present, monitor clinically for weakness and arrhythmia.
Are parasites present? Positive → treat with albendazole or praziquantel; reduces malabsorption. If lab unavailable, give empiric deworming in endemic areas.
Is HIV positive? Guides need for ART, cotrimoxazole prophylaxis, and higher calorie targets. If unavailable, assess risk factors and consider presumptive ART per national guidelines.

sections.p: Classification follows WHO/UNICEF criteria for children and WHO adult GAM thresholds, supplemented by clinical signs for chronic malnutrition.
b: Adults: Severe acute malnutrition – BMI <16 kg/m² or MUAC <22 cm (men) / <23 cm (women).
Adults: Moderate acute malnutrition – BMI 16‑16.9 kg/m² or MUAC 22‑22.9 cm (men) / 23‑23.9 cm (women).
Children 6‑59 mo: Severe acute malnutrition – MUAC <11.5 cm or WHZ <‑3 SD or oedema present.
Children 6‑59 mo: Moderate acute malnutrition – MUAC 11.5‑12.5 cm or WHZ between ‑3 and ‑2 SD.
Stunting (chronic) – Height‑for‑age <‑2 SD in children <5 yr; indicates long‑term undernutrition.
Kwashiorkor – Edematous malnutrition with normal/low weight, hypoalbuminaemia, skin lesions; classified as severe acute.
Marasmus – Non‑edematous severe wasting; BMI <16 kg/m² or MUAC <22 cm in adults.

sections.p: Several diseases mimic malnutrition; careful history, targeted tests and distinguishing signs separate them.

t.b: Points: peripheral edema, cachexia, dyspnoea. Separate by cardiac auscultation, BNP, echocardiogram; edema in heart failure is often bilateral with raised JVP.
Points: anorexia, weight loss, oedema, anaemia. Distinguish with serum creatinine, eGFR, urine protein; CKD edema is often pitting with high urea.
Points: rapid weight loss, tremor, tachycardia, heat intolerance. Separate with TSH and free T4; thyroid storm shows elevated heart rate disproportionate to malnutrition.
Points: intentional food restriction, low mood, lack of infection. Diagnose via mental‑status exam; labs usually normal except low weight.
Points: chronic diarrhoea, weight loss, iron deficiency. Confirm with tissue transglutaminase IgA and duodenal biopsy; improves with gluten‑free diet.
Points: night sweats, cough, weight loss, low‑grade fever. Diagnose with GeneXpert, sputum smear, chest X‑ray; treat TB to reverse wasting.

sections.p: A structured ladder ensures safe, effective care of malnutrition, from immediate stabilization to definitive therapy and timely escalation.
b: 1. Immediate assessment: vital signs, capillary glucose, hydration status, edema, and nutritional intake
2. Stabilise hypoglycaemia with 10% dextrose bolus (5 mL/kg) if capillary glucose <3 mmol/L; avoid 50% dextrose to prevent osmotic injury
3. Initiate re‑feeding cautiously: start with 10–20 kcal/kg/day, increase by 10–20 kcal/kg/day over 3–5 days; monitor electrolytes
4. Provide micronutrient supplementation: vitamin A, zinc, folate, thiamine, selenium; give thiamine before carbohydrate loading
5. Choose nutrition route: oral therapeutic foods (RUTF) for mild–moderate; nasogastric feeding for severe or when oral intake inadequate; TPN only if gut non‑functional
6. Monitor daily: weight, MUAC, oedema, serum electrolytes (phosphate, potassium, magnesium), glucose, renal function
7. Escalate: if persistent hypoglycaemia, worsening oedema, electrolyte derangement, or failure to gain weight, consider higher energy formula, enteral feeding, or TPN
8. Refer: severe acute malnutrition with oedema, re‑feeding syndrome, or complications (e.g., septic shock, fistula) to tertiary care

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key medications used in malnutrition carry specific adverse effects and interactions that must be anticipated and managed.
b: 1. Dextrose solutions: risk of hyperglycaemia, hypokalemia, and osmotic diuresis; monitor glucose and electrolytes
2. Thiamine: rare anaphylaxis; give before carbohydrate loading to prevent Wernicke’s encephalopathy
3. Zinc: high doses can cause copper deficiency; monitor copper levels if long‑term therapy
4. Vitamin A: hypervitaminosis A causes hepatotoxicity and intracranial hypertension; avoid in acute liver failure
5. Antiretrovirals (e.g., zidovudine): can worsen anaemia and neutropenia; monitor blood counts
6. Anti‑TB drugs (rifampicin, isoniazid): hepatotoxicity; monitor LFTs and adjust nutrition to avoid fatty liver
7. Herbal remedies (e.g., neem, African potato): potential hepatotoxicity and drug interactions; inquire about use and monitor LFTs

sections.p: Recognising early complications allows timely intervention and prevents deterioration.
b: 1. Re‑feeding syndrome: hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, arrhythmias; treat with phosphate, potassium, magnesium, thiamine
2. Edema: indicates hypoalbuminaemia or heart failure; assess with serum‑ascites albumin gradient if ascites present
3. Electrolyte imbalance: monitor daily; treat promptly to avoid cardiac arrhythmias
4. Infections: high risk in malnourished; monitor temperature, WBC, CRP; start empiric antibiotics if sepsis suspected
5. Wasting and sarcopenia: progressive muscle loss; reassess nutrition plan and consider anabolic agents if indicated
6. Liver dysfunction: monitor bilirubin, transaminases; avoid hepatotoxic drugs and high‑fat formulas

sections.p: Underlying conditions modify presentation, investigations and treatment of malnutrition.
b: 1. HIV: increases protein catabolism, alters drug metabolism; avoid rifampicin‑based regimens if severe malnutrition; monitor CD4 and viral load
2. TB: chronic inflammation lowers albumin; use hepatoprotective nutrition
3. Pregnancy: increased energy needs; use RUTF or high‑protein formulas; monitor fetal growth
4. Diabetes: risk of hypoglycaemia with re‑feeding; use low‑glycaemic index foods
5. Renal failure: restrict potassium and phosphate; adjust dextrose concentration
6. Liver failure: avoid high‑fat formulas; monitor LFTs closely
7. Alcohol: increases nutrient loss; counsel on abstinence; avoid hepatotoxic drugs
8. Age extremes: infants need higher protein; elderly may have reduced appetite; tailor caloric density accordingly
9. Herbal remedies: potential hepatotoxicity; review all supplements

sections.p: Tailored approaches are essential for children, pregnant women, the elderly, HIV patients and low‑resource settings.
b: 2. Pregnancy: MUAC <18.5 cm severe; provide 1.5–2 kcal/kg/day extra; monitor fetal growth with ultrasound
3. Elderly: assess sarcopenia; use protein‑dense formulas; monitor for frailty and falls
4. HIV patients: integrate ART initiation with nutrition; monitor for drug–nutrient interactions; use high‑protein RUTF
5. Low‑resource settings: rely on MUAC and weight‑to‑height; use ready‑to‑use therapeutic foods; avoid expensive labs; use clinical signs for re‑feeding syndrome

sections.p: Sample questions to test comprehensive knowledge of malnutrition management.

t.a: A 3‑year‑old presents with MUAC 12 cm and weight loss 15% over 4 months. What is the next step?
t.b: Assess hydration, check capillary glucose, start RUTF and monitor weight daily

t.a: A 45‑year‑old HIV‑positive man with BMI 15 kg/m² has peripheral oedema. What laboratory test is most useful?
t.b: Serum albumin and electrolytes; low albumin suggests hypoalbuminaemia, but consider inflammation

t.a: Why is 10% dextrose preferred over 50% for hypoglycaemia in malnutrition?
t.b: Lower osmolarity reduces risk of osmotic injury and hyperglycaemia

t.a: What micronutrient should be given before carbohydrate loading in severe malnutrition?
t.b: Thiamine to prevent Wernicke’s encephalopathy

t.a: A malnourished child develops vomiting after starting RUTF. What is the likely complication?
t.b: Re‑feeding syndrome; check phosphate, potassium, magnesium and give thiamine

t.a: A patient on TPN develops cholestasis. What is the likely cause?
t.b: Long‑term TPN causing liver dysfunction; consider lipid reduction and enteral feeding

t.a: Why is nasogastric feeding preferred over oral therapeutic foods in a patient with a high‑output fistula?
t.b: It allows complete bowel rest and precise caloric delivery while bypassing the fistula

t.a: Which drug interaction is most concerning when giving rifampicin to a severely malnourished patient?
t.b: Induction of cytochrome P450 leading to reduced efficacy of other drugs and increased hepatotoxicity

t.a: A pregnant woman with severe malnutrition has MUAC 17 cm. What is the recommended energy intake?
t.b: Add 1.5–2 kcal/kg/day to baseline; use high‑protein RUTF

facts: BMI <16 kg/m² or MUAC <22 cm (men) / <23 cm (women) = severe acute malnutrition in adults
BMI 16–16.9 kg/m² or MUAC 22–22.9 cm (men) / 23–23.9 cm (women) = moderate acute malnutrition in adults
Serum albumin <30 g/L is a negative acute‑phase reactant, not a reliable sole marker of nutrition
Refeeding hypoglycaemia treated with 10% dextrose bolus (5 mL/kg) if capillary glucose <3 mmol/L

vivas.q: What bedside measurement would you use to screen for acute malnutrition in a 3‑year‑old child?
vivas.a: Measure mid‑upper arm circumference; MUAC <13.5 cm flags possible acute malnutrition.

vivas.q: How does chronic malaria contribute to malnutrition and what investigations would you order?
vivas.a: Malaria causes anaemia, loss of appetite and protein loss; order haemoglobin, ferritin, malaria smear, and assess for anaemia causes.

vivas.q: Why is serum albumin not a reliable sole marker of nutritional status in an acutely ill patient?
vivas.a: Albumin is a negative acute‑phase reactant; it falls with infection, inflammation or fluid shifts, masking true nutritional status.

vivas.q: When would you choose nasogastric feeding over oral therapeutic foods in a malnourished patient?
vivas.a: When the patient cannot tolerate oral intake, has a high‑output fistula, or requires complete bowel rest.

vivas.q: Identify two micronutrients most commonly deficient in East African malnutrition and their clinical features.
vivas.a: Vitamin A – night blindness, xerophthalmia; Zinc – growth retardation, impaired wound healing.

vivas.q: What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent referral for a malnourished child with suspected refeeding?
vivas.a: Severe hypokalaemia, seizures, or cardiac arrhythmia – signs of refeeding syndrome.

vivas.q: Distinguish between protein‑energy malnutrition and wet beriberi in an alcoholic patient.
vivas.a: PEM shows muscle wasting, oedema, hypoalbuminaemia; wet beriberi shows oedema with normal albumin, tachycardia, and peripheral neuropathy.

vivas.q: A 52‑year‑old woman with an enterocutaneous fistula has persistent tachycardia and fevers despite TPN. What is the likely cause?
vivas.a: Ongoing fistula output causing fluid and protein loss; consider fistula‑related sepsis or inadequate output control.

vivas.q: For a high‑output proximal small bowel fistula requiring complete bowel rest, what is the preferred route of nutrition?
vivas.a: Total parenteral nutrition via central venous access.

vivas.q: An infant with an omphalocele has a central venous line placed for monitoring and parenteral nutrition. Which specialized line can also be left safely in place during the repair?
vivas.a: A peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) can be left in situ during surgery.

vivas.q: After oesophageal atresia repair, a contrast leak is identified on day 6. What is the immediate nutritional management?
vivas.a: Stop enteral feeds, start parenteral nutrition, and monitor for sepsis.

vivas.q: An infant on TPN develops direct hyperbilirubinaemia and conjugated jaundice. Which aspect of ongoing management should be reviewed?
vivas.a: Check for line sepsis, TPN lipid content, and consider reducing TPN duration or switching to enteral feeds.

vivas.q: An infant with massive bowel resection develops parenteral nutrition‑dependent intestinal failure, liver dysfunction, and line sepsis. What overarching long‑term condition should be addressed?
vivas.a: Intestinal failure‑associated liver disease; consider early transition to enteral feeds and monitor liver function.

vivas.q: A 50‑year‑old postoperative patient on nasogastric enteral nutrition develops frequent liquid stools. What is the most common gastrointestinal complication?
vivas.a: Diarrhoea due to rapid gastric emptying and osmotic load of the formula.

vivas.q: A 38‑year‑old man with severe burns requires nutritional support. Why is enteral feeding preferred over parenteral nutrition when the gut is functional?
vivas.a: Enteral feeding maintains gut integrity, reduces bacterial translocation, and is cost‑effective.

vivas.q: Discuss the indications and baseline requirements before starting total parenteral nutrition.
vivas.a: Indications: inability to meet needs enterally, severe malnutrition, high‑output fistula. Baseline: electrolytes, glucose, liver/kidney function, infection screen, central line assessment.

vivas.q: Discuss the placental roles and how placental dysfunction or prematurity affects fetal protection and nutrition.
vivas.a: Placenta supplies oxygen, nutrients, and hormones; dysfunction leads to intrauterine growth restriction and long‑term metabolic disease.

vivas.q: Outline the schedule and components of growth monitoring and nutrition surveillance for children from birth to 5 years.
vivas.a: Monthly weight and MUAC for 0–2 years, quarterly thereafter; record height/length, weight‑for‑age, MUAC, and dietary intake.

mcqs.q: A 6‑month‑old child presents with weight loss and MUAC 12.0 cm. What is the first‑line therapeutic milk?
mcqs.e: F‑75 is the low‑protein therapeutic milk for severe malnutrition.

mcqs.q: Which micronutrient should be given before carbohydrate re‑introduction in a severely malnourished patient?
mcqs.e: Thiamine prevents Wernicke’s encephalopathy during refeeding.

mcqs.q: A patient with severe malnutrition develops hypokalaemia after starting feeds. What is the most likely cause?
mcqs.e: Refeeding syndrome causes intracellular shift of potassium.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a WHO cut‑off for severe acute malnutrition in children 6–59 months?
mcqs.e: Weight‑for‑age <80% is not a WHO cut‑off for SAM.

mcqs.q: A 45‑year‑old HIV patient with BMI 15 kg/m² and oedema is started on RUTF. Which drug should be given immediately?
mcqs.e: Thiamine prevents Wernicke’s encephalopathy during refeeding.

mcqs.q: Which investigation is most useful to differentiate hypoalbuminaemia due to malnutrition from that due to protein loss?
mcqs.e: SAG distinguishes loss from decreased synthesis.

mistakes: Confusing MUAC cut‑offs for children and adults
Treating low albumin as proof of severe malnutrition
Delaying thiamine until after carbohydrate re‑feeding
Giving iron immediately in severe malnutrition
Over‑reliance on BMI alone for adult malnutrition assessment
Ignoring the need for central line assessment before TPN
Assuming RUTF is suitable for all age groups without dose adjustment
